title: The Indoor Winter
briefing: Mira, 15, is a gymnast who trains in an indoor gym all winter. She drinks three glasses of milk a day because her coach says bones need calcium. But her coach also tells the whole team to get outside in the daylight on weekends — “milk alone isn't enough.”
question: If the calcium is in the milk, why would sunlight matter for her bones?

clues.title: Plenty of milk
clues.text: Mira drinks three glasses of milk every day. Milk has lots of calcium, the main building material in bone.
clues.shows: plenty of calcium going into her body

visual.unit: glasses of milk a day, last year → now

clues.title: Dark mornings, dark evenings
clues.text: In winter she leaves for school before sunrise and leaves the gym after dark. For six weeks her skin has seen almost no daylight.
clues.shows: her skin getting almost no sunlight

clues.title: A page in her textbook
clues.text: Her biology book says skin cells make vitamin D when sunlight falls on them. Very little is made in winter.
clues.shows: the skin acting as a vitamin D factory that needs daylight

clues.title: The gut needs a key
clues.text: The same page says vitamin D helps the gut take calcium in from food. Without enough of it, much of the calcium passes straight through.
clues.shows: calcium needing vitamin D before the body can absorb it

hypotheses.text: Bones only need calcium, so drinking even more milk will fix everything.
hypotheses.flaw: Clue 4 says the gut can't take in much calcium without enough vitamin D, so calcium alone can't fix it — and the small amount of vitamin D added to milk isn't enough without daylight.

hypotheses.text: Sunlight warms the bones and that makes them stronger.
hypotheses.flaw: Bones are deep inside the body; what sunlight does is let the skin make vitamin D — a chemical, not warmth.

hypotheses.text: Indoor air is bad for bones.
hypotheses.flaw: Nothing about air reaches the bones. What is missing indoors is daylight on her skin.

hypotheses.text: Her skin makes vitamin D only in sunlight, and vitamin D lets her gut absorb calcium — so with almost no sun, much of the milk's calcium isn't taken in.

prediction.prompt: It's winter. As Mira spends more hours outdoors in daylight each week, how much vitamin D does her skin make?

second.question: With the same hours outside in summer instead, would her skin make more or less?

concepts.label: sunlight / daylight
concepts.hint: What was missing from Mira's winter?

concepts.label: vitamin D
concepts.hint: What does the skin make in sunlight?

concepts.label: the gut absorbs calcium
concepts.hint: Why isn't drinking the milk enough on its own?

concepts.label: calcium builds bones
concepts.hint: What do the bones actually need to be built from?

transfer.context: Two classes drink the same amount of milk at lunch. One class has PE outdoors all year; the other has PE in a basement gym with no windows.
options: The outdoor class takes in more calcium, because sunlight on their skin makes vitamin D, which helps the gut absorb it.
Both classes take in the same calcium, because the milk is the same.
The basement class takes in more, because they rest their bones.
Neither — calcium from milk can't be absorbed.
transfer.retryHint: Same milk, different daylight — which of Mira's clues says what daylight does to calcium?
transfer.explanation: The milk is the same, but only the outdoor class's skin is making much vitamin D. Vitamin D is what lets the gut take calcium in, so the outdoor class absorbs more of the very same milk.

takeaway: Bones are built from calcium, but the gut needs vitamin D to take calcium in — and skin makes vitamin D in daylight. Food and sunlight work as a team.
